title: What the 2026 Midterm Election Results Mean for U.S. Refugee Policy
subtitle: What a new Congress could change in refugee funding and admissions, and which decisions remain with the president.

content.caption: The east front of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on 1 May 2026.

content.text: Prior to the final vote count, it seemed that the Democrats had a chance to win both chambers. According to FiftyPlusOne on November 3, the probability of Democratic control of the House of Representatives was 99% and that of the Senate was 79%. These probabilities refer to control of each chamber rather than to the percentage of the vote cast.

The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats on November 3 and the House of Representatives on November 4. The Democrats will take control at the beginning of the new term starting on January 3, 2027. The interim measures of funding passed prior to the election will stay in force until December 11, or until replaced by new legislation. Thus, the outgoing Congress will have to make a decision on funding.

Congress has a right to change legislation on immigration, fund the programs, and to check actions of the executive branch of government. The main question is what powers the Democrats will have to influence refugee admissions policy while the incumbent president remains in office. The cap, suspension of entry, and funding are regulated by different laws. Election results cannot influence these laws directly. The proposal will need to indicate which laws are to be changed and the passing of the proposal will depend on votes.

content.text: Legal Bases of the 17,500 Cap of Admissions

By his decision of September 25, 2026, the president set the refugee admission cap for fiscal year 2027 at 17,500, the major part of which is allocated to Afrikaners from South Africa. This is a maximum number with no obligation to fill all places. Additional restrictions exist due to executive orders and directives. The executive order No. 14163 suspended the entry of refugees. An allocation under the cap does not ensure admission of refugees.

The ceiling of refugee admissions per year is set according to Section 207 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). It is determined by the president after discussion with Congress, when the data on refugees' needs, allocations, and associated costs are presented. However, it does not mean that the judiciary committees have the right to either approve or disapprove this decision through consultation. Thus, the change of members of these committees does not itself change the decision of September 25, 2026.

The authority to issue Executive Order 14163 is based on Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which gives the president the right to suspend entry to the USA if he finds entry detrimental to U.S. interests. The considerations of national security, available resources, assimilation, and responsibilities of states and local governments are mentioned. The secretaries of State and Homeland Security may jointly, at their discretion, authorize an individual’s admission if it serves the national interest and does not threaten U.S. security or welfare.

On May 3, 2021, President Biden used emergency powers given in Section 207(b) and increased the cap of annual admission from 15,000 to 62,500. On May 21, 2026, President Trump, using the same Section 207(b), raised the ceiling of FY2026 from 7,500 to 17,500 and allocated extra places to Afrikaners. Congress may try to negotiate a new decision with the president, but the mandatory increase in the cap will require the new law.
Funding considerations in December

December 11 will be the deadline for the upcoming funding decision of the outgoing Congress. Congress may agree on a new deal or on prolongation of interim funding. In case of the prolongation which will be extended to the period after January 3, the next decision could fall to the next Congress. A deal covering the whole year would settle more spending for fiscal year 2027 before Democrats take control. Both of these decisions give Congress the possibility to pass the new legislation later.

The current temporary funding measure generally keeps funding levels of fiscal year 2026 and the conditions which existed at that time. The measure restricts initiation or resumption of programs and activities without corresponding fiscal year 2026 appropriation, funds or authorization. A proposal to expand processing must clarify which accounts will be used, how they may be used, and which terms will need exceptions. December 11 is not the expiration date for all appropriations on refugee matters.

The majority will give Democrats the chance to pass the new legislation and to perform committee work. But to pass any proposal, Congress has to approve it in both chambers and to submit it to the president. The president has the right to sign or to veto this bill. The veto may be overridden by a two-thirds majority in each chamber. Having the majority does not mean that the veto will be overridden.

However, in the Senate there exists one more aspect of distinction between the majority and the bill approval. Three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn, usually 60, are generally needed to end debate on ordinary legislation. Cloture is not identical to the final voting on the bill. Even in case of majority support, it may be stopped on the procedural basis. The idea that the new majority can automatically overturn the admissions policy ignores this procedure and veto power of the president.

Congress has a right to negotiate appropriations which set the spending and impose the conditions and requirements on distribution of some funds. Congress may also change the underlying admissions legislation. Conditions of appropriations are applicable only to funds and periods specified in the act. The statutory amendment can set the continuing requirement. The draft must specify clearly its impact because only an increase of funding does not eliminate the president's entry suspension authority.
Oversight and evidence

The admissions legislation provides a basis for comprehensive review. According to Section 207(d), reports on the global refugee situation and proposals of admissions must be submitted before each fiscal year. Progress in admissions and possible reallocations are periodically discussed with the judiciary committees. According to Section 207(e), information about proposals of admissions, countries of origin, cost, domestic impacts, and involvement of other countries must be submitted. The new committee chairmen may use these requirements to conduct hearings regarding specific decisions.

One of the issues is the population selection for admissions. The government could be asked to explain the evidence supporting allocation of places to Afrikaners, assessment of other populations, and how this selection corresponds to statutory categories. Congress may review these criteria and evidence without assuming that nationality alone makes people eligible.

Another issue is exceptions to the entry suspension. Congress may request summarized statistics of the number of requests, decisions made, approvals issued, and number of arrivals. The breakdown by period and stages of processing may help to detect delays. The sensitive information in individual files must be protected. An increase in approvals does not necessarily mean an increase in arrivals when travel is pending.

Oversight may distinguish refugee admissions from asylum. According to Section 208, individuals in the USA or arriving at its borders may apply for asylum according to the statutory requirements and restrictions. Asylum decisions under Section 208 do not count against the cap on U.S. refugee admissions under Section 207. Combining these numbers can complicate the distinction between the policies evaluated and the laws requiring amendments.

The decision of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in the case of Pacito v. Trump dated March 5, 2026, is an example of the drafting problem. In reviewing appeals on preliminary injunctions, the court recognized wide presidential authority on the suspension of refugee entry and reversed some points of preliminary injunctions concerning admissions, processing, and overseas funding. The court interpreted Section 207 as setting a cap and not as a minimum number of admissions. The opinion does not resolve the dispute completely.

It means that for people who want to end the entry suspension, an increase of the cap alone could be insufficient. Thus, the legislative proposals must clarify the relation between Sections 207 and 212(f), besides any new obligations lawmakers impose on officials concerning processing. Lawmakers may also consider whether modification is required in rules on exceptions, deadlines, and judicial review. If these questions are ignored, an increase in the cap can coexist with the same restrictions which now do not allow entry.
